key_facts: Benign, ill-defined, **non-scaly pale macules** merging on the trunk; no itch or prior inflammation.
Common in young adults, especially with darker skin; slowly progressive, may improve after mid-life.
Wood's lamp often shows **follicular red fluorescence** (*Cutibacterium acnes*).
Differentials: pityriasis versicolor (fine scale, yeast), PIH, vitiligo (chalk-white), leprosy (numb).
Options with variable evidence: benzoyl peroxide ± clindamycin, NB-UVB, oral tetracycline; relapse is common.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: PMH is an acquired, **benign** condition of ill-defined, **non-scaly** hypopigmented macules. They often merge into patches on the trunk. It is **asymptomatic**, with no itch, pain or preceding inflammation. It progresses slowly over years and may stabilise or improve after mid-life.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: The cause is not fully known. The leading hypothesis is **Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes** in the hair follicles producing a depigmenting factor. This is supported by **follicular red fluorescence** under a Wood’s lamp in many, but not all, patients. Genetic factors may contribute.
Melanin is reduced while melanocyte numbers are normal, and melanosome packaging is altered on electron microscopy.

ul: **"It's fungal, so antifungals will fix it"**: it doesn't scale and doesn't respond.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: A follicular bacterium is thought to **reduce melanin production** in nearby skin.

mech.t: Bacteria in follicles may produce a depigmenting factor.
Melanocyte numbers stay normal but melanin falls.
Melanosome packaging changes on electron microscopy.

ul: Round or oval, **poorly bordered** pale macules that merge on the back and trunk, with or without the proximal limbs and neck.
**No scale.** This is the key difference from pityriasis versicolor.
**No preceding rash.** This is the key difference from post-inflammatory hypopigmentation.
More noticeable, and more often reported, in **darker skin**. Typically teens and young adults, possibly more common in women.
Clinical.
**Wood’s lamp:** follicular **coral-red** fluorescence supports *C. acnes*.
**Skin scrapings (KOH) are negative**, unlike pityriasis versicolor.
Dermoscopy shows ill-defined white macules with a faint pigment network. Biopsy is rarely needed.

ddx.name: Pityriasis versicolor
ddx.f: **Fine scale**; ‘spaghetti and meatballs’ on KOH; often yellow-green under Wood’s lamp

ddx.name: Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation
ddx.f: History of eczema, psoriasis or another rash at the same sites

ddx.name: Vitiligo
ddx.f: Sharp, **chalk-white** patches, often on the hands, face and around orifices; bright white under Wood’s lamp

ddx.name: Pityriasis alba
ddx.f: Faces of atopic children; mild scale

ddx.name: Hypopigmented mycosis fungoides
ddx.f: Persistent, atypical, progressive patches in an adult. **Refer**

ddx.name: Ash-leaf macules (tuberous sclerosis)
ddx.f: Congenital, leaf-shaped; look for other features of tuberous sclerosis

ul: **Reassure** that it is benign. Explain the *C. acnes* theory and the slow course.
Options with **variable evidence**: topical **benzoyl peroxide ± clindamycin**, **narrowband UVB** (specialist), oral **tetracyclines**, or combinations. Isotretinoin appears only in case reports.
Relapse after stopping treatment is common.
Refer to dermatology if the diagnosis is uncertain, or if the patient wants treatment for cosmetic reasons.

refer.t: Atypical, persistent or progressive patches in an adult: exclude **hypopigmented mycosis fungoides**.
Congenital or ash-leaf-shaped macules with other signs: consider **tuberous sclerosis**.
‘Pityriasis versicolor’ that does not respond to antifungals: re-check for scale and do KOH.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Atypical, persistent or progressive patches in an adult: exclude **hypopigmented mycosis fungoides**.
Congenital or ash-leaf-shaped macules with other signs: consider **tuberous sclerosis**.
‘Pityriasis versicolor’ that does not respond to antifungals: re-check for scale and do KOH.
Cosmetic concern.
Slowly progressive; may stabilise.

pearls: Do not keep treating it as ‘fungus’. If there is scale, take a **KOH scraping first**.
Photoprotection still helps even out skin tone.
Manage expectations: response is **slow and often incomplete**.

quiz.q: When should you think of Progressive macular hypomelanosis (PMH)?
quiz.a: Poorly defined, non-scaly, symptom-free pale macules merging on the back and trunk of a teenager or young adult, often with darker skin.
Probably Cutibacterium acnes in the follicles producing a depigmenting factor. Melanin is reduced but melanocyte numbers are normal.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Reassure. Options with variable evidence: benzoyl peroxide ± clindamycin, narrowband UVB, oral tetracycline.
Persistent, atypical, progressive patches in an adult may be hypopigmented mycosis fungoides. Refer.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Atypical, persistent or progressive patches in an adult: exclude **hypopigmented mycosis fungoides**.
